title: A Quality Assessment of Information Available on Renal Cancer on YouTube
screen_reason: Cross-sectional content analysis of the first 120 eligible YouTube videos returned for the search term 'kidney cancer' (September 2021). Two urologist authors independently rated each video, with a third as tie-breaker, judging accuracy against the current EAU or AUA renal-cell-carcinoma guidelines, and scored a 5-point misinformation scale. The paper reports the SHARE of videos containing misinformation (49.2%; 22.5% at moderate-to-high level) with a stated denominator, which meets the CONTENT criterion. The DISCERN and GQS results are also reported as shares and are recorded as QUALITY rows, excluded from prevalence.

estimates.country: Not restricted; English-language YouTube videos, 77.5% created in North America, 13.3% Europe, 6.7% Asia, 2.5% other
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube 'kidney cancer' videos rated as containing any misinformation (misinformation Likert score >= 2), judged against EAU/AUA guidelines
estimates.value_raw: 49.2% (Discussion) / '49.7% of the videos analysed' (Results); Table 4 misinformation score: 1 = 61 (50.8%), 2 = 32 (26.7%), 3 = 18 (15%), 4 = 7 (5.8%), 5 = 2 (1.7%), n = 120
estimates.denominator: 120 YouTube videos returned by the search 'kidney cancer' (default relevance sort) that met inclusion criteria: English, duration > 1 minute, > 500 views, renal cancer addressed; drawn from >4,000 videos identified and 250 saved for review
estimates.definition: Video scored 2 or higher on a 5-point misinformation Likert scale (1 = good quality information with low levels of misinformation, 5 = high levels of misinformation); accuracy judged by consistency with the latest European Association of Urology or American Urological Association guidelines. The authors treat score 1 as 'no misinformation'.
estimates.misinfo_def: No conceptual definition of misinformation is given. Operationally: “Information on the accuracy of information was assessed on the basis of consistency with either the latest European Association of Urology or American Urological Association guidelines” and “Misinformation was assessed using a 5-point Likert scale. On this scale, a score of 1 point indicated good quality information with low levels of misinformation, and a score of 5 points indicated high levels of misinformation.”
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was found in 49.7% of the videos analysed, and 22.5% contained moderate to high levels of misinformation. The other 50.3% were scored as having no misinformation. ... Our analysis found that there was a significant proportion of videos with misinformation (49.2%).
estimates.page_loc: Results p. 317 and Discussion p. 318; Table 4
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two authors (both clinicians, J.S. and R.S.) independently reviewed all 120 videos; a third author (D.A.) held the deciding vote on any discrepancy. Accuracy benchmarked against EAU or AUA renal cell carcinoma guidelines, with a literature search for videos covering alternative therapies. NO inter-rater reliability statistic (no kappa, no percent agreement) is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The term “kidney cancer” was used to search YouTube (www.YouTube.com) in September 2021. ... The default search setting on YouTube was used, which automatically sorts the videos by relevance. We included all videos that were in English, had over 500 views, and covered information on renal cancer. ... The first 120 videos meeting these criteria were included in the study.
estimates.notes: BORDERLINE between CONTENT and QUALITY, and the reason matters. It is coded CONTENT because the accuracy judgment is guideline concordance made by clinician raters - which the protocol lists as a valid external ground truth - and because the instrument is explicitly a misinformation scale rather than DISCERN/GQS. But the scale's own anchor for the lowest score is 'good quality information with LOW levels of misinformation', not 'none', so a wholly accurate but incomplete or outdated video could plausibly be scored 2, and the 50.8% at score 1 are only retrospectively described as having 'no misinformation'. The stricter >= 3 variant row is the safer estimate. NUMBER DISCREPANCY: the Results text says 49.7% and 'the other 50.3%', which is internally inconsistent and does not match Table 4 (61/120 = 50.8% at score 1, so 59/120 = 49.2% at score >= 2). The Discussion's 49.2% is the value consistent with the table, so it is the one recorded. Denominator is a rank-truncated first-120 relevance-sorted set with a >500-view floor, so it represents what a searcher would plausibly see, not the population of kidney-cancer videos.

estimates.country: Not restricted; English-language YouTube videos, 77.5% created in North America
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube 'kidney cancer' videos rated as containing MODERATE TO HIGH levels of misinformation (Likert score >= 3)
estimates.denominator: The same 120 included YouTube videos on kidney cancer
estimates.definition: Video scored 3, 4 or 5 on the 5-point misinformation Likert scale, i.e. moderate, high or extreme levels of misinformation relative to EAU/AUA guidelines
estimates.misinfo_def: “Misinformation was assessed using a 5-point Likert scale. On this scale, a score of 1 point indicated good quality information with low levels of misinformation, and a score of 5 points indicated high levels of misinformation.”
estimates.source_quote: Misinformation was found in 49.7% of the videos analysed, and 22.5% contained moderate to high levels of misinformation. ... Of these, 22.5% scored between moderate and extreme levels of misinformation.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same dual independent clinician rating with third-author adjudication against EAU/AUA guidelines; no reliability statistic reported.
estimates.notes: Stricter threshold variant of the row above; 22.5% is stated verbatim twice and matches Table 4 exactly (27/120). The Discussion's phrasing 'Of these, 22.5%' is loose - 22.5% is a share of all 120 videos, not of the 49.2% with any misinformation, as the table confirms. This is the more defensible of the two thresholds for a prevalence synthesis.

estimates.country: Not restricted; English-language YouTube videos, 77.5% created in North America
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube 'kidney cancer' videos scoring moderate to high (>= 3) on the modified DISCERN reliability tool
estimates.value_raw: 74.1% of all videos were of moderate to high (>= 3) reliability; 25.9% low or very low. Table 4 DISCERN: 1 = 14 (11.7), 2 = 17 (14.2), 3 = 42 (35), 4 = 28 (23.3), 5 = 19 (15.8); median 3
estimates.denominator: The same 120 included YouTube videos on kidney cancer
estimates.definition: Video scored 3 or more of 5 on the modified DISCERN tool (aims clear; reliable sources used; information balanced and unbiased; additional sources listed; areas of uncertainty stated)
estimates.misinfo_def: n/a - DISCERN measures reliability/quality of presentation, not veracity
estimates.source_quote: The modified DISCERN indicated a high number of videos scoring as moderate quality of information with an overall median score of 3; 74.1% of all videos in the study were of moderate to high (>= 3) reliability. However, a significant portion of the videos (25.9%) were of low or very low quality.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two independent clinician raters with third-author adjudication; modified DISCERN is a 5-item checklist, not a veracity judgment. No reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The modified DISCERN tool is scored based on 5 questions with 1 point for each answer ... With 1-2 points indicating low quality, 3 points indicating moderate quality and 4-5 points indicating high overall quality.
estimates.notes: QUALITY row - a wholly accurate video that simply fails to list sources or state uncertainty scores low, so this cannot be read as misinformation prevalence. Kept for the quality appendix only. Table 4 gives 89/120 = 74.2% at >= 3, trivially different from the stated 74.1%.

estimates.country: Not restricted; English-language YouTube videos, 77.5% created in North America
estimates.measure_type: % of YouTube 'kidney cancer' videos rated moderate to excellent on the Global Quality Score
estimates.value_raw: 83.4% moderate to excellent; 24.2% excellent; 16.6% poor or generally poor. Table 4 GQS: Poor 7 (5.8), Generally poor 13 (10.8), Moderate 38 (31.7), Good 33 (27.5), Excellent 29 (24.2)
estimates.denominator: The same 120 included YouTube videos on kidney cancer
estimates.definition: Video rated moderate, good or excellent on the 5-point Global Quality Score, which grades usefulness of the information to the intended audience
estimates.misinfo_def: n/a - GQS measures usefulness to patients, not veracity
estimates.source_quote: The GQS tool indicated that 83.4% of the videos had moderate to excellent levels of quality; 24.2% of the videos scored as excellent for the content they provided. A proportion of the studies (16.6%) were scored either poor or very poor for levels of information.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Same two independent clinician raters with third-author adjudication; GQS grades usefulness, not accuracy. No reliability statistic reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: The GQS was based on a 5-point scale including poor quality (not useful for patients), generally poor quality (very limited use), moderate quality (somewhat useful), good quality (useful for patients), and excellent quality (very useful for patients).
estimates.notes: QUALITY row, excluded from prevalence: a usefulness rating says nothing about truth or falsity. Table 4 gives 100/120 = 83.3% at moderate-or-better, trivially different from the stated 83.4%.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (a) Median misinformation score (2), median DISCERN (3) and median GQS (moderate), including the pre-/post-2016 subgroup medians - scale MEANS/medians with no share attached; the protocol bars them. (b) 24.2% deemed to have commercial bias and 5.8% with COI disclosures - commercial bias is a conflict-of-interest judgment, not a veracity classification. (c) Content descriptives (39.2% hospital/clinic publishers, 60% doctor presenters, 62.4% intended for patients, 34.2% gave an overview, 29% of treatment videos discussed side effects, 19% included intraoperative scenes) - composition of the corpus, not misinformation. (d) '17% of the YouTube videos included in their study on bladder cancer showed commercial bias' (Loeb et al.) - a figure cited from another paper, barred by R8. (e) The pre-2016 vs post-2016 misinformation split (Table 4 columns) is a time split within the same corpus, not a distinct estimate; the paper reports it as counts with identical medians and a P value, and collapsing to the overall figure follows the time-series rule. INTERNAL INCONSISTENCIES worth flagging to the review: the Results state 49.7% / 50.3% while Table 4 and the Discussion give 50.8% / 49.2%; the number of videos found is given as 'over 4000' in Results and 'over 7000' in the Discussion; Table 2's intended-audience percentages sum to more than 100 (37.5 + 14.2 + 62.4 + 7.2) and the text quotes 14.7% where the table says 14.2%; the text says median comments 5 where Table 1 says 7. The misinformation numbers used here are the table-consistent ones.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis. Single search term ('kidney cancer') in September 2021, default relevance sort; inclusion required English, >1 minute, >500 views and renal cancer content; duplicates, advertisements, instructional surgical videos and videos lacking audio excluded. The first 120 qualifying videos of >4,000 identified (250 saved to a playlist) were analysed - a rank-truncated convenience set. Two clinician authors rated every video independently with a third as tie-breaker; accuracy benchmarked against EAU/AUA guidelines. No inter-rater reliability statistic of any kind is reported. Instruments: modified DISCERN (5 items), Global Quality Score (5-point), and a 5-point misinformation Likert scale. Analysis descriptive plus two-sample t tests. Authors acknowledge single-platform limitation and rapid platform change.
rob.item6_quote: Misinformation was assessed using a 5-point Likert scale. On this scale, a score of 1 point indicated good quality information with low levels of misinformation, and a score of 5 points indicated high levels of misinformation.
rob.item10_quote: Misinformation was found in 49.7% of the videos analysed, and 22.5% contained moderate to high levels of misinformation. The other 50.3% were scored as having no misinformation.
